comparison: Both strongly support the core finding of correspondence between fractal and classical cycles (C42-C50). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor with correlation coefficients (r=0.4-0.5) and Bayesian analysis across 940 cycles. Peer reviewers confirm 81% one-to-one matching and R≈0.5 correlation, calling it 'solid evidence.' Both treat this as the foundational validation of the fractal cycle method.

Both support age-related differences showing shorter cycles in children (C53-C56). OpenEval notes appropriate statistical testing with medium effect sizes but flags small pediatric sample (n=21). Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms 'shorter cycles in children' as a key demonstration of validity. Both treat this as evidence the method tracks developmental differences.

Both support clinical utility in MDD showing longer cycles with REM-suppressive antidepressants (C65-C72). OpenEval provides detailed effect sizes (d=0.3-0.7) across n=111 patients with medication-specific effects. Peer Reviewer 1 confirms 'longer cycles in patients medicated with REM-suppressing anti-depressants' as valid demonstration of clinical utility. No challenges from either evaluation.

Both support skipped cycle detection performance (C57-C60, C7). OpenEval highlights 91-98% detection rate comparable to human inter-rater agreement (91%). Peer reviewers accept the high detection rate as supporting evidence without challenge. Both treat this as validation of algorithm performance, though peer review provides less detailed analysis.

Contrasting evaluations of age effects on fractal cycles (C61-C64). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to weak correlations (r=-0.16 to -0.19) and speculative mechanisms. Peer Reviewer 1 treats this positively as an advantage: 'fractal method identifies a correlation between age and cycle duration in adults that is not apparent with the classical method.' Peer review frames as strength while OpenEval emphasizes limitations.

Both support mechanistic explanations for fractal-classical discrepancies (C51-C52, C78). OpenEval finds correlational evidence statistically significant and biologically plausible. Peer Reviewer 1 contextualizes discrepancies as 'tied to the uncertain definition of sleep cycles' and cycle boundary ambiguity, accepting these as methodological differences rather than errors. Both frame discrepancies as understandable.

Perfect agreement on methodological benchmarking (C89-C91). Both support that fractal-classical correspondence is comparable to automatic-manual classical cycle correspondence. OpenEval notes this suggests fractal approach 'not inferior to existing automated methods.' Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'discrepancies between the two are on the order of that found between classical cycles defined manually or via an automatic algorithm,' contextualizing moderate correlation as acceptable.

Both support main conclusions (C106-C108) but with nuanced differences. OpenEval emphasizes objectivity, quantifiability, and biological plausibility demonstrated across datasets. Peer reviewers call it 'valuable' and 'novel' with 'solid evidence,' but Reviewer 1 cautions 'unlikely that fractal scoring will be able to replace classical scoring directly,' suggesting complementary use. OpenEval more unequivocally supportive of the method's potential.

Partial overlap on overnight dynamics (C73-C75). OpenEval groups these with broader validation claims about fractal-classical correspondence. Peer review separately acknowledges fractal cycles span whole night and distinguishes wake from sleep cycles. Both accept these characterizations without challenge, though peer review gives less detailed treatment.

Both address wake/REM similarity (C77). OpenEval includes this in mechanistic explanation for discrepancies, noting smoothed slopes show similar values. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'from the fractal cycle perspective, waking and REM sleep are not very dissimilar' and notes this 'underlies some of the key results.' Both accept this observation as valid.

Partial overlap on fractal cycle advantages (C84-C85). OpenEval supports advantages over SWA including lower inter-individual variability and whole-night cycling, though notes reliance on prior work. Peer review implicitly accepts whole-night cycling characterization. Limited direct comparison in peer review on these specific advantages.

Both address skipped cycle mechanism (C92). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN overall, finding C92's mechanistic explanation reasonable but C93 purely speculative. Peer review accepts skipped cycle detection results without detailed mechanistic discussion. OpenEval more cautious about extending beyond tested applications.

Different perspectives on age effect mechanisms (C95). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting weak correlations, non-linearities, and unclear mechanisms requiring further investigation. Peer review frames age correlation as an advantage of fractal method over classical. OpenEval focuses on mechanistic uncertainty while peer review emphasizes detection capability.

OpenEval evaluates theoretical foundation claims (C29-C38) as SUPPORTED, noting extensive prior literature citations provide biological plausibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific theoretical/background claims, though peer reviewers implicitly accept the conceptual framework.

OpenEval rates speculative mechanistic interpretations (C87-C88, C109-C115) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are explicitly marked as speculation and neurotransmitter hypotheses require human validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found directly addressing these speculative mechanism claims.

OpenEval rates MDD mechanistic explanations and insomnia pilot findings (C101-C105) as UNCERTAIN, noting speculative interpretations and pilot data requiring replication. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these mechanistic explanations, though peer review accepted the overall MDD findings.
